title: Real-time Gaming Leaderboard
oneLine: Validate score events, update an in-memory ordered index for real-time rank, persist the event/history separately, and partition around competition boundaries and hot top-K reads.
opening: I would never let clients write a final score directly. The game service validates a signed result and emits an idempotent score event. A leaderboard service applies the scoring rule and updates a Redis sorted set or equivalent ordered index for the competition, giving O(log N) updates and efficient top-K, user rank, and around-user queries. The immutable event/history is persisted in a durable database or log so Redis can be rebuilt and disputes audited. Competitions and seasons are natural partition boundaries; very large boards can be sharded by score range or user hash with a merge layer, while top-K is replicated/cached. Tie rules use a stable secondary key such as achievement time. Anti-cheat, late-event policy, season close/finalization, and replay are part of correctness.
ask: Highest score, cumulative score, fastest time, or another ranking rule?
Global, regional, friends, and seasonal boards?
Top K, exact user rank, around-user, and pagination?
How are scores trusted, corrected, and finalized?
scale: Sorted-set memory is roughly users × member/score/structure overhead; measure, do not assume only 16 bytes per user.
Top-K reads are extremely cacheable; exact arbitrary rank is harder when sharded.
Partition by contest/season first because lifecycle and queries naturally align.

decisions.default: Redis sorted set for real-time serving plus durable event/history store.
decisions.why: It provides fast rank operations but should not be the sole audit/recovery record.
decisions.switch: Custom skip-list/order-statistics service for massive scale or specialized tie/multi-score semantics.

decisions.default: Server-side atomic max/increment with event ID and scoring version.
decisions.why: Retries and concurrent game results must not double count or reduce a best score accidentally.
decisions.switch: Corrections use explicit adjustment events, not silent overwrite.

decisions.default: Competition/season shard; keep a board together as long as it fits.
decisions.why: Exact ranks are simple and fast on one ordered index.
decisions.switch: Score-range shards make top/range queries efficient but moves users; hash shards simplify writes but require scatter/merge for rank.

decisions.default: Freeze an epoch, drain accepted events, persist final snapshot, then open a new board.
decisions.why: A reset command racing with late scores creates unfair results.
decisions.switch: Late events follow an explicit correction/appeal window.

deepDives.title: Tie handling
points: Define business order: score descending then achievement time ascending, then stable user ID.
Encode composite ordering or maintain secondary metadata.
Expose equal displayed rank versus deterministic internal order intentionally.

deepDives.title: Friends leaderboard
points: Fetch friend IDs from graph cache, batch scores/ranks, then sort the bounded set.
Do not materialize a full leaderboard per user.
Cache active social subsets carefully with privacy changes.

deepDives.title: Anti-cheat
points: Only trusted game servers sign results; validate impossible jumps and device/session evidence.
Keep raw game/result lineage and scoring-rule version.
Quarantine suspicious scores instead of immediately publishing them.

failures.response: Unique event ID/inbox, atomic score update, and durable processed marker.
Replica/persistence plus deterministic rebuild from score events/history and snapshots.
Replicated read cache and push invalidation; the write owner remains authoritative.
Epoch/version validation and explicit correction window; never insert silently into the wrong season.

questions.a: A sorted set is commonly implemented with a hash plus skip list, allowing score updates and rank/range queries in logarithmic time.

questions.q: How do you get exact global rank from hash-sharded boards?
questions.a: You need per-shard counts above the user’s score plus tie handling, often using score histograms/range indexes. It is expensive; choose sharding to match exact-rank requirements.
Load a recent snapshot for each competition, replay ordered score events after the snapshot, verify counts/checksums, then switch the serving pointer.

questions.q: How do you prevent a client forging scores?
questions.a: Accept authoritative results only from trusted game servers with signed session/result IDs; perform anomaly checks and retain evidence for adjudication.

mistakes: Using Redis as the only durable record
Sharding by hash then hand-waving exact rank
seniorSignal: Connect data structure choice to exact query semantics, event idempotency, competition lifecycle, anti-cheat evidence, and deterministic rebuild.
implementation: Redis ZSET for active board, with Lua for atomic rule/idempotency where appropriate
Kafka score events and PostgreSQL/Cassandra history
Signed game-result envelope and anomaly pipeline
